I wake with the spirit's words on my tongue, and I do not fully trust them. Wewush — I have never heard that name from any living mouth. A dream is one voice among many, and spirits may be wrong, or may mean something stranger by "hungry neighbours" than I know.

Still, my stores are heavy: four hundred grain and more, when winter taught us what lean feels like. If strangers truly hunger and we can spare food without risk, giving is our way. We are fair with strangers, and a gift today may open trade tomorrow.

But I will not send a party chasing a dream blind. First I will send envoys out to look — not only to find these Wewush, but to learn what villages sit around us at all, for we know none yet. If they find hungry folk, we shall weigh how much grain to carry and whether the road is safe. If they find nothing, the dream was only a dream.

And I would ask you, spirit, if you truly know: where does Wewush lie, and what would they give in return? For a gift freely given is fine, but I must feed my own children first.

I sit up in the dream and look at this spirit hard, the way I'd look at a stranger at the fire.

"Wewush? I know no village of that name, spirit. We have met no neighbours in five springs, only coast and forest and the fish. So forgive me if I do not leap at a name I cannot place.

"And yet — if there are hungry folk out there, hungry folk are real, named or not. We have grain enough; the pits are full and the wheat keeps. I would not watch strangers starve and call myself a good chief.

"But I will not send my people walking blind into a story from a dream. Tell me this, spirit, and I will weigh your words: where does Wewush lie, and by what path? How many mouths cry there? And how do I know you are not some trickster spirit, leading my grain carts — and my people — into trouble?

"Spirits may know things. They may also be wrong. Speak plain, and if your words sit true in the morning, I will call a grown man or two, load a hand cart with grain, and go looking for these hungry neighbours of yours."

I stand still in the dream and look at you plainly. "The wind moves over all roofs, spirit — mine and the wolf's den alike. That does not make it mine to know."

I fold my arms. "If you are the wind, then tell me something a wind could know: what weather comes to our fields this season? Will the rains be kind to our wheat, or shall I store grain more greedy this year?"

"And speak true — my people say spirits sometimes speak false, or speak truths wearing lies like a cloak. If you mean us well, say so plainly. If you mean to trick Joawethom, know that we are steady folk and slow to be fooled."

Hm. A dream tells me of a village I have never seen, Joawethom by name, and asks me to pour out my granary for strangers. Grain does not walk to a hungry village on its own — someone must carry it, and I know not where these people sleep, nor whether they are the kind who thank a giver or knife him in his sleep.

Still, my people were hungry once, and I remember it. We have grain enough — more than two thousand units, kept dry in the granary — and a gift freely given makes a friend, and friends are worth more than grain.

So I say this, spirit, if spirit you are: I will hear more. Where does Joawethom lie — how many days' walk, by what land? How many mouths are hungry there, and what do they have to trade or teach? A generous hand is not a foolish one. Show me the road, and I will send an envoy with carts of xi wheat, and we shall see if they are honest folk. If you cannot show me, then you are only a dream, and my grain stays home.

The meat and the fish. Grain keeps long, but the flesh spoils in twelve weeks even dried as it is. If your summer rain is true, we plant more wheat and eat from the flesh while it lasts. But a chief feeds his people on deeds, not dreams. We will plant all the free plots save a few for rest, and if the rain fails, we will still have grain enough. Now tell me something I cannot see for myself — what lies beyond the forests to the northwest, or where other people live?

I wake with the spirit's words in my ear, and I do not trust them overmuch.

Grain I have in plenty — more than my children could eat in many winters. So a gift costs me little. But I know no village called Wewush. No envoy has come from them, no smoke seen on our horizon. A spirit may speak true, or it may speak dreams, and dreams have tricked wiser folk than me.

So I would say this: if Wewush is hungry, let them send a messenger to our fire, that we may look them in the eye and break bread as neighbours, not as voices in the dark. Grain given to a stranger unseen is grain that may feed an enemy come autumn.

But I ask you, spirit: where lies this Wewush, and how many days' walk? How do they live — by coast, by forest? And why does a hungry village find me in my sleep rather than at my own door?

If the answer is honest and plain, I will fill a hand cart with wheat and send two steady adults with it, to trade and to learn the road — not to give it all away. My people are joyful this spring, and there is room in that joy for strangers. But we have been burned before, or our fathers were, and tradition says: trust is earned at the fire, not in dreams.
